The opposite of explode, array to string conversion.
To beg or plead for (something) earnestly or urgently; to beseech.
d.x: And giue me leaue, / And doe not ſay 'tis Superſtition, that / I kneele, and then implore her Bleſſing.

d.g: To beg or plead that (someone) earnestly or urgently do something; to beseech, to entreat.
d.x: Acquaint her vvith the danger of my ſtate, / Implore her, in my voice, that ſhe make friends / To the ſtrict deputie: […]

d.g: Often followed by for (a thing) or of (a person): to express an earnest or urgent plea.
d.x: That fortnight Rochester passed in intriguing and imploring.

implore.e: PIE word *h₁én The verb is borrowed from Middle French implorer (modern French implorer (“to beg, plead, implore”)), or directly from its etymon Latin implōrāre, the present active infinitive of implōrō (“to beseech, entreat, implore; to appeal to, pray to”), from im- (a variant of in- (intensifying prefix)) + plōrō (“ …

d.g: To have as a necessary consequence; to lead to (something) as a consequence.
d.x: Correlation does not imply causation

d.g: To suggest by logical inference.
d.x: When I state that your dog is brown, I am not implying that all dogs are brown.

d.g: To hint; to insinuate; to suggest tacitly and avoid a direct statement.
d.x: What do you mean "we need to be more careful with hygiene"? Are you implying that I don't wash my hands?

imply.e: From Middle English implien, emplien, borrowed from Old French emplier, from Latin implicare (“to infold, involve”), from in (“in”) + plicare (“to fold”). Doublet of employ and implicate.

d.g: To bother, irritate, trouble.
d.x: To deliberate, be it but in slight matters, doth importune me.

d.g: To harass with persistent requests.
d.x: You were kneel'd to, & importun'd otherwiſe / By all of vs; […]

d.g: To approach to offer one's services as a prostitute, or otherwise make improper proposals.

importune.e: From Middle French importuner and its etymon Medieval Latin importūnor (“to make oneself troublesome”), from Latin importūnus (“unfit, troublesome”), originally "having no harbor".

d.g: To apply, enforce, or establish (something, often regarded as burdensome as a restriction or tax: see verb sense 1.2.2) with authority.
d.x: Congress imposed new tariffs.

d.g: To place or put (something chiefly immaterial, especially something regarded as burdensome as a duty, an encumbrance, a penalty, etc.) on another thing or on someone; to inflict, to repose; also, to place or put (on someone a chiefly immaterial thing, especially something regarded as burdensome).
d.x: Social relations impose courtesy.

d.g: To force or put (a thing) on someone or something by deceit or stealth; to foist, to obtrude.
To subject (a student) to imposition (“a task inflicted as punishment”).

impose.e: The verb is derived from Late Middle English imposen (“to place, set; to impose (a duty, etc.)”), borrowed from Middle French imposer, and Old French emposer, enposer (“to impose (a duty, tax, etc.)”) (modern French imposer), from im-, em- (variants of en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’)) + poser (“to place, put”), modelle …

d.g: To shut up or place in an enclosure called a pound.
d.x: His car was impounded after he parked it illegally.

d.g: To hold back.
d.x: water impounded by a dam

d.g: To hold in the custody of a court or its delegate.
d.x: to impound stray cattle

d.g: To collect and hold (funds) for payment of property taxes and insurance on property in which one has a security interest.

impound.e: Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English im- English pound English impound From im- + pound.

d.g: To make poor.
To weaken in quality; to deprive of some strength or richness.
d.x: That exuberant crop quickly impoverishes any fertile soil.

d.g: To become poor.

impoverish.e: From Middle English empoverishen, impoverishen, empoverischen, enpoverisshen, Anglo-Norman empoveriss-, from Old French empoverir, from em- + povre, from Latin pauper (“poor”) (English poor).

d.g: To call down by prayer, as something hurtful or calamitous.

imprecate.e: Borrowed from Latin imprecātus, perfect active participle of imprecor (“to invoke (good or evil) upon, pray to, call upon”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“upon”) + precor (“to pray”).

d.g: To cause to become pregnant.
d.x: I was impregnated at a clinic but don't know who the sperm donor is.

d.g: To fertilize.
To saturate, or infuse.
d.x:

 To impregnate with tartar.

d.g: To fill pores or spaces with a substance.

impregnate.e: The adjective is first attested in 1540, the verb in 1605; borrowed from Medieval Latin impraegnātus, perfect passive participle of Latin impraegnō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of impregn; participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

d.g: To put in or as if in prison; confine somebody against their will.
d.x: [...] demand for the boots fell sharply after the Battle of Waterloo, and Brunel was imprisoned for debt in 1821.

imprison.e: Inherited from Middle English imprisonen, emprisounen, emprisonen, from Old French emprisonner. Equivalent to im- + prison.

d.g: To make (something) better; to increase the value or productivity (of something).
d.x: Painting the woodwork will improve this house.

d.g: To become better.
d.x: I have improved since taking the tablets.

d.g: To use or employ to good purpose; to turn to profitable account.
d.x: to improve one's time;  to improve his means

improve.e: From Anglo-Norman emprouwer, from Old French en- + prou (“profit”), from Vulgar Latin prode (“advantageous, profitable”).

d.g: To make something up or invent it as one goes on; to proceed guided only by imagination, intuition, and guesswork rather than by a careful plan.
d.x: He had no speech prepared, so he improvised.

improvise.e: From French improviser; ultimately from Latin improvisus.

d.g: Alternative spelling of improvise.
To verbally assault, especially to argue against an opinion, motive, or action; to question the truth or validity of; cast doubt on.
d.x: For quotations using this term, see Citations:impugn.

impugn.e: Borrowed from Middle French impugner, from Latin impugnō, from im- + pugnō (“fight”), from pugnus (“fist”), as in English pugilism (“fighting with fists, boxing”).

d.g: To attribute or ascribe (responsibility or fault) to a cause or source.
d.x: The teacher imputed the student's failure to his nervousness.

d.g: To ascribe (sin or righteousness) to someone by substitution.
To take into account.
To attribute or credit to.
d.x: People impute great cleverness to cats.

impute.e: Borrowed from Middle French imputer, from Latin imputō (“to bring into the reckoning, charge, impute”).
